questions.question: Distinguish between current, capital and transfer expenditure with one example of each. Explain how revenue is divided between the three spheres.
questions.expected_answer: Current expenditure is on items used up within the year, e.g. teachers' salaries, medicines, interest. Capital expenditure is on assets lasting many years, e.g. building schools, clinics, roads. Transfer payments are made with nothing received in return, e.g. social grants. The Division of Revenue Act divides nationally raised revenue: national government keeps a share for its functions (defence, police, higher education, grants); provinces receive an equitable share (by formula, mainly learners and health needs) plus conditional grants; local government receives an equitable share and infrastructure grants.

questions.question: Describe what government spends on in each of the six CAPS areas: education, health, housing, social grants, transport and security.
questions.expected_answer: Education: teachers' salaries, no-fee schools, school nutrition, school buildings, universities, TVET colleges, NSFAS. Health: public hospitals and clinics, staff, medicines, vaccines, HIV treatment, free primary health care. Housing: subsidised (RDP/BNG) houses, informal settlement upgrading, serviced sites, First Home Finance. Social grants: child support, older person's, disability, foster child, care dependency grants and the SRD grant, paid by SASSA. Transport: national, provincial and municipal roads, commuter rail, bus subsidies, road safety. Security: police, courts and justice, correctional services, defence force.

questions.question: In an illustrative budget of R1 000, education receives R300 and health R200. Calculate each share. If the budget rises to R1 100 and the extra R100 goes to health, calculate health's new share. Explain the opportunity cost of rising debt-service costs.
questions.expected_answer: Education: 300 ÷ 1 000 × 100 = 30%. Health: 200 ÷ 1 000 × 100 = 20%. New health share: 300 ÷ 1 100 × 100 ≈ 27,3%. Debt-service costs are interest on government borrowing; every rand paid in interest cannot be spent on education, health, housing, grants, transport or security, so rising interest crowds out services. This is the opportunity cost of past borrowing.
